lesson.title: Independent Assortment: Shuffling Two Genes at Once
lesson.summary: Mendel's law of independent assortment states that alleles of genes located on different chromosomes are sorted into gametes independently of one another, because homologous chromosome pairs line up and separate independently during meiosis I, a pattern that breaks down for genes linked closely together on the same chromosome.
lesson.body:
The law of segregation, covered in the previous chapter, describes what happens to the two alleles of a single gene during gamete formation. The law of independent assortment goes a step further and describes what happens when two or more genes are tracked at the same time. It states that the alleles of one gene are sorted into gametes independently of the alleles of another gene, provided the two genes sit on different chromosomes.

The physical basis for this rule follows directly from the chromosomal theory of inheritance. During metaphase I of meiosis, each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up at the metaphase plate independently of every other pair. Whether the maternal or paternal copy of one chromosome ends up facing a given pole has no bearing on whether the maternal or paternal copy of a different chromosome faces that same pole. Because of this independent orientation, an individual who is heterozygous for two genes on different chromosomes produces all four possible combinations of alleles among its gametes, in equal proportions. This is one of two reasons, alongside crossing over, that gametes end up genetically unique, as noted in the gametes chapter.

It is important to be precise about where this law applies. Independent assortment holds for genes on different chromosomes. It does not hold, at least not fully, for genes that sit close together on the same chromosome. Such genes are said to be linked, because there is no independent chromosome movement available to separate them, they travel together into the same gamete far more often than chance alone would predict. Only crossing over, covered earlier, can separate linked genes, and it does so less frequently the closer together the two genes sit on the chromosome. So independent assortment is best understood as a consequence of independent chromosome behavior specifically, not a universal rule that applies to every pair of genes regardless of location.

Mendel's own dihybrid pea experiments provide a worked example, using two genes that behave as though they sit on different chromosomes: seed shape, with R for round, dominant, and r for wrinkled, recessive, and seed color, with Y for yellow, dominant, and y for green, recessive. A plant that is doubly heterozygous, RrYy, produces four types of gametes in equal proportion, RY, Ry, rY, and ry, since segregation applies to each gene independently and the four combinations follow from combining the two 1 to 1 splits. Crossing two RrYy plants together and combining these gametes produces offspring in the classic ratio of 9 round yellow to 3 round green to 3 wrinkled yellow to 1 wrinkled green, the well known 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 ratio that is the signature result of independent assortment acting on two genes at once. Notice that each trait considered on its own still follows the familiar 3 to 1 pattern from the law of segregation, round to wrinkled works out to 3 to 1, and yellow to green also works out to 3 to 1. Independent assortment simply says that these two 3 to 1 patterns combine freely with each other, rather than being tied together, because the genes for seed shape and seed color sit on different chromosomes.
